design_detail: Open within-person laboratory study with brain imaging. 15 healthy volunteers were recruited, each to have a baseline [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan and two drug scans a month apart, in randomised order, with two of three drugs (racemic ketamine, psilocybin or d-amphetamine); 5 had ketamine and psilocybin, 5 ketamine and d-amphetamine, 5 psilocybin and d-amphetamine, so the ketamine analyses rest on 10 people. This report covers only the ketamine condition. Ketamine (Ketalar, Parke Davis) was given intravenously as 20 mg in 20 ml saline over 5 min, then 5 min with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min for 60 min, with the infusion started 10 min before the FDG injection. Psychopathology was rated with the APZ, AMDP and EPI scales for the scan period; cerebral glucose metabolism (CMRglu) was measured in 18 regions of interest per hemisphere on Talairach coordinates and expressed as absolute values, relative values (region divided by whole-brain mean) and ratios between regions; arterial plasma ketamine was measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry at five time points. All tests were Wilcoxon matched-pairs tests and Spearman correlations, with no correction for multiplicity.
can_establish: Whether a subanesthetic intravenous ketamine infusion changes psychopathology ratings and cerebral glucose metabolism, in 10 healthy volunteers compared with their own drug-free baseline scan, and which regional pattern that change takes.
cannot_establish: Any effect attributable to the drug rather than to expectancy or to the scanning situation, since the study was open, there was no placebo condition and each person had already had a preliminary drug session; the size or robustness of any symptom-metabolism association (correlations in 10 people, reported as P-levels only, uncorrected, which the authors call preliminary); anything about repeated or longer-term use, about people who use ketamine outside the laboratory, or about people with psychiatric illness; and anything outlasting the session, since all measurements were made during or immediately after the infusion.

sample.recruitment: University and hospital staff, examined at the Research Department of the Psychiatric University Hospital of Zurich, the MRI Center of the University Hospital of Zurich and the PET Department of the Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen (p. 10).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy volunteers screened by psychiatric interview for absence of personal and first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder; anyone with a history of non-medical use of illicit drugs was excluded (the paper uses the older term); the openness and neuroticism scales of the Freiburg Personality Inventory were also used as an exclusion criterion; physical examination, electrocardiogram, blood and urine analysis normal, and a normal MRI (p. 10). The study was approved by the hospital ethics committee and the use of psychoactive drugs by the Swiss Federal Health Office (p. 10).
sample.demographics: The 15 recruited were 8 men and 7 women aged 26 to 43 (mean 33.3, SD 4.8). The 10 who received ketamine, listed individually in Table 1, were 6 men and 4 women with a mean age of 33.40 (SD 3.57), FPI openness 8.50 (SD 2.76) and neuroticism 3.10 (SD 1.73), against the normative means printed in the table footnote. No education, occupation, tobacco, alcohol or caffeine data (pp. 10-11).
sample.attrition: None reported; all 10 who received ketamine appear in Table 1 and in the analyses, and no withdrawal is mentioned.
sample.selection_effects: Staff of the hospital and university, screened to be psychiatrically and physically healthy, with no history of non-medical drug use, selected in part on personality scores, and prepared by a preliminary drug session. Colleagues of the investigators are not a neutral group for self-rated effects in an open study, and the sample tells nothing about people who use ketamine outside the laboratory or about people with psychiatric illness.

exposure.measurement: Drug given and measured in the laboratory: arterial plasma ketamine by a gas chromatography-mass spectrometry method with a stated sensitivity of 10 ng/ml, sampled through the radial artery cannula at 0, 10, 30, 48 and 54 min, stored at -20 degrees; the levels in Table 1 are the means of those 5 samples (pp. 11, 13-14).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as printed: ketamine (Ketalar, Parke Davis, Switzerland) intravenously, 20 mg in 20 ml saline over 5 min as an induction step, then 5 min with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min for 60 min by infusion pump; the infusion was started 10 min before the FDG injection so that peak effect would coincide with the start of the scan. One ketamine session per person (pp. 11-12).
exposure.polysubstance: Within the study design, 5 of the 10 also had a psilocybin scan and 5 a d-amphetamine scan, each at least a month from the ketamine scan; the results of those conditions are reported elsewhere. No concurrent medication, tobacco, alcohol or caffeine use is reported, and nothing is said about what participants consumed on scan days.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. No pre-scan toxicology or abstinence requirement is described; scans were a month apart and participants arrived at the PET department at 11 a.m. (p. 12).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own baseline FDG-PET scan, performed on a separate day. The baseline is drug-free, not a placebo: no sham infusion is described, and the study is called an open study (p. 10). No separate control group and no group of people with psychiatric illness.
comparison.matching: Within-person design; baseline and drug scans were performed in randomised order across participants, with no randomisation method, concealment or period-effect analysis described (p. 10).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense, because each person is their own baseline. What is unmeasured is expectancy: participants knew they would receive a stimulant or a hallucinogenic drug (p. 10), the study was open, and the preliminary drug session means nobody was drug-naive at the PET scan.

outcomes.instruments: Psychopathology, referring to the phase during the PET scan: the Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire (APZ), self-rated, with a global score and three subscales, oceanic boundlessness (OSE, derealisation and depersonalisation with positive mood), dread of ego dissolution (AIA, loss of autonomy and self-control with anxiety and paranoid feelings) and visionary restructuralization (VUS, illusions and pseudo-hallucinations, synesthesia, changed meaning of percepts); the Ego Pathology Inventory (EPI), rated by an experienced psychiatrist, with a global score and five subscales (ego identity, demarcation, consistency, activity, vitality); and the AMDP inventory, giving schizophrenic and manic-depressive syndrome scores and the subscales apathy, thought disorder and hallucinatory-disintegration. Imaging: [18F]FDG PET on a CTI Siemens 933/04-16 tomograph, 8 mm in-plane resolution, 12 planes, mean administered FDG dose 177.6 MBq (min 107.3, max 244.2), 23 arterial samples, the autoradiographic method of Rhodes et al., transformation to Talairach space, standardised regions of interest (5.6-10.4 mm) placed symmetrically in both hemispheres with the coordinates shown in Fig. 1; absolute CMRglu in micromol per 100 g per min, relative CMRglu and metabolic gradients between two regions of the same hemisphere (pp. 11-13).
outcomes.validity_norms: The three APZ dimensions are cited as empirically derived and validated in an international study of altered states (n=1133) and as independent of what induced the state; the EPI is cited as measuring five empirically derived dimensions of ego pathology; FPI normative means are printed in the Table 1 footnote. No norms for the AMDP, and no reliability data for any rating in this study. Regional values come from hand-placed standardised regions of interest, not from voxelwise statistics.
outcomes.operationalization: Nothing is operationalised as harm or impairment. The model psychosis is operationalised as the change from the baseline scan in self-rated and psychiatrist-rated scale scores; hyperfrontality is operationalised as an increase in absolute and relative frontal CMRglu and in frontal-to-posterior and frontal-to-subcortical ratios, the ratio method being taken from published work on people with schizophrenia.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, and none is mentioned anywhere in the paper. The count of about 150 is the editors' tally of the comparisons displayed or reported: 32 regional absolute CMRglu tests (Fig. 3) and 32 relative tests (Fig. 4), the whole-brain test, 32 ratio tests (Table 2, 16 ratios by 2 hemispheres), about 12 region-against-region comparisons of the size of the increase and 5 hemispheric asymmetry tests (p. 14), 11 psychopathology comparisons (Fig. 5), the correlations in Table 3 and in the text, and the correlations of plasma level with metabolism and with syndrome scores. Unlike its companion paper, this one does not warn the reader that the analysis is exploratory, except for the statement that the correlational results are preliminary because of the small sample (p. 21).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None, and none is claimed: the study is described as open (p. 10). The psychiatrist who rated the AMDP and EPI, the person placing the regions of interest and the analysts are not described as blind, and participants knew the design.

analysis.effect_sizes: Almost none: results are percentage changes from baseline with Wilcoxon P-levels, except the whole-brain change, which is given as 24.5% with an SD of 14.3 (P<0.01), and Table 2, which prints means and SDs of the ratios under both conditions. Correlations appear only as P-levels with a sign (Table 3). No confidence intervals and no test statistics. Editors' calculations: the whole-brain increase of 24.5% (SD 14.3, n=10) corresponds to a 95% confidence interval of about 14.3% to 34.7% and a standardised paired difference of about 1.7; the ratio increases recomputed from the means in Table 2 are about 9.6% (left) and 9.4% (right) for frontomedial/occipitomedial and about 9.9% and 8.5% for frontomedial/temporomedial.
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted within-person comparisons; relative CMRglu and ratios are used instead of adjustment to remove global and between-person variation (pp. 13-14).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome. The stated hypothesis is that psychotomimetic ketamine doses would activate the frontal cortex in association with positive and negative symptoms (p. 10).
analysis.selective_reporting: Substantial. Of 18 regions per hemisphere, 16 are plotted in Figs. 3 and 4 and only some appear numerically in the text; Table 3 shows 5 of the 16 ratios; one correlation is given as data not shown (p. 21); the psilocybin and d-amphetamine conditions of the same participants are reported elsewhere, so the full set of comparisons made in this programme cannot be seen from this paper. Several values exist only in figures, from which exact numbers cannot be read.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. The authors state that the correlational results are only preliminary because of the small sample (p. 21). With 10 participants and paired non-parametric tests the smallest attainable two-sided P is 0.002.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 10 healthy volunteers who knew they were receiving a drug, a subanesthetic ketamine infusion was followed by an acute psychosis-like state on all three rating scales and by higher glucose metabolism in every participant, largest in the anterior cingulate and frontal cortex (30-34%) and smallest in the occipitomedial cortex (16-17%), so that frontal-to-temporal, frontal-to-occipital and frontal-to-subcortical ratios rose. The correlations between symptom scores and metabolism are uncorrected, based on 10 people, reported only as P-levels with a direction, and go in both directions depending on the scale: the ego-pathology measures correlated positively with frontomedial metabolism, while the hallucinatory-disintegrative subscale correlated negatively with it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that increased metabolic activity in the frontomedial and anterior cingulate cortex correlated positively with psychotic symptom formation, in particular with ego pathology (p. 9). The ego-pathology half is supported (oceanic boundlessness with right frontomedial CMRglu, P<0.03; ego identity with the left frontomedial/anterior cingulate ratio, P-level 0.03 in Table 3), but the same Results report the opposite sign for the other half of the psychosis construct: the hallucinatory-disintegrative subscale correlated negatively with absolute and relative frontomedial CMRglu in both hemispheres (P<0.05, p. 15) and the schizophrenic syndrome score correlated negatively with the frontomedial/occipitomedial ratios (p. 15), facts the abstract does not mention. The further claim that the findings support increased frontal metabolism in acutely psychotic patients (p. 21) is a comparison with published studies, not with patients studied here. The authors are careful in two respects that anyone citing this paper should keep: they call the correlational analysis preliminary because of the small sample (p. 21) and they limit the model to the beginning of acute psychotic episodes, "not for schizophrenia as a nosological entity" (p. 21). The whole design also leaves expectancy uncontrolled, which the paper nowhere discusses.

timeline.event: Krystal et al. report dose-related psychotomimetic, perceptual and cognitive effects of subanesthetic ketamine in healthy volunteers, cited here as the comparison for the symptom profile

Lahti et al. report increased frontomedial and anterior cingulate blood flow with an exacerbation of positive symptoms when ketamine was given to people with schizophrenia stabilized on haloperidol (as cited in this paper, pp. 20-21; not appraised here)

Companion paper from the same laboratory, in a different sample of 10 healthy volunteers, finds the same hyperfrontal pattern with (S)-ketamine and the opposite, mainly downward, pattern with equimolar (R)-ketamine

A meta-analysis of functional neuroimaging studies of ketamine in healthy volunteers is listed in the project source list (Ait Bentaleb et al.) and has not yet been appraised; it is the place to check whether the hyperfrontality finding holds across tracers, tasks and analysis methods

replication.where_it_stands: That a subanesthetic ketamine infusion produces a short-lived psychosis-like state in healthy volunteers was already established when this paper appeared and is not in doubt. The specific finding here, a global rise in glucose metabolism with a frontal maximum, was found again by the same laboratory with (S)-ketamine in a different sample, which is consistency within one group rather than independent replication, and both studies were open or effectively unblinded. The symptom-metabolism correlations are the weakest part and were not stable even between the two companion papers, as the authors themselves note. Whether the hyperfrontality result survives in later imaging work, which mostly used blood flow or BOLD rather than FDG, is a question for the neuroimaging meta-analysis on the project list, not yet appraised.

funding.funder: Supported in part by the Swiss National Research Foundation (32-28746.90) (p. 21).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: University and national-laboratory setting (Psychiatric University Hospital of Zurich; Paul Scherrer Institute). No industry sponsor is named; the drug was a commercial preparation obtained from Parke Davis (Switzerland) (p. 11).

what_would_settle_it: A within-person study of the same kind with a genuine placebo infusion, a tested blind (participants and raters asked what they believed they received, with guessing reported), randomised order with period effects modelled, a pre-specified primary outcome and correction for multiplicity, and voxelwise imaging analysis with enough participants to estimate symptom-metabolism associations with confidence intervals rather than P-levels alone.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of baseline and drug scans)
domains.note: Order is stated to have been randomised across participants but no method, sequence generation, concealment or allocator is described (p. 10); which of the two other drugs each person received is not said to have been randomised either.

Scans were a month apart, so pharmacological carryover is unlikely, but no period or order effect is examined, participants had had a preliminary drug session, and 5 of the 10 also had a psilocybin scan and 5 a d-amphetamine scan within the same series.

The study is described as open (p. 10): there is no placebo condition, the comparison is a drug-free baseline scan, and neither participants nor the rating psychiatrist were blind. Self-rated APZ scores and psychiatrist-rated AMDP and EPI scores are therefore made in full knowledge of the condition, and the metabolic comparison is between a drug day and an ordinary day.
All 10 participants who received ketamine appear in Table 1 and in the analyses; no missing data are reported.

PET quantification is objective, but regions of interest were hand-placed on standardised coordinates with no stated blinding and no reliability data, and the psychopathology ratings are partly retrospective: the APZ was completed after the session and refers to the scan period, while the AMDP and EPI were rated around the scan (pp. 12-13).

No protocol, about 150 displayed comparisons with no multiplicity correction, selective reporting of regions, ratios and correlations, one correlation given as data not shown (p. 21), and two further drug conditions in the same participants reported elsewhere.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person design and the consistency of the metabolic change (whole-brain CMRglu rose in every participant) make the direction of the metabolic finding credible, and the psychopathological change is large on three scales. The overall judgment is set by the open, placebo-free design, in which expectancy is uncontrolled for both self-rated and observer-rated outcomes, and by the selective reporting of many uncorrected comparisons. The source can be cited for: the psychopathological and metabolic profile of a subanesthetic ketamine infusion at the stated rates in healthy volunteers; the size and regional pattern of the glucose-metabolic increase; plasma concentrations during such an infusion and the time to the first psychotic symptoms; and the authors' own limitation of the model to the start of acute psychosis. It cannot be cited for any drug-specific effect net of expectancy, for the size of any symptom-metabolism association, for a causal statement about which brain region produces which symptom, or for any claim about effects outside the session.

key_findings.finding: 15 healthy volunteers (8 men, 7 women, aged 26-43, mean 33.3, SD 4.8) were recruited from university and hospital staff for an open study of three conditions, each person having a baseline scan and two drug scans a month apart in randomised order; 5 received ketamine and psilocybin, 5 ketamine and d-amphetamine and 5 psilocybin and d-amphetamine, so the ketamine results come from 10 people.
key_findings.locator: Experimental procedures, Subjects (2.1) and Experimental design (2.2)

key_findings.finding: Ketamine was given intravenously as 20 mg in 20 ml saline over 5 min, then 5 min with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min for 60 min; the infusion began 10 min before the FDG injection so that the peak effect would coincide with the start of the scan.
key_findings.locator: Experimental procedures, text following Table 1 (p. 11); Phase II: PET studies (2.6), 2nd paragraph (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Plasma ketamine levels ranged from 240 to 1145 ng/ml (mean 557, SD 254, the mean of 5 samples per person); psychotic symptoms appeared on average 4.5 min after the start of administration at a mean plasma level of 386 ng/ml. Plasma levels did not correlate significantly with whole-brain or regional metabolic change, but correlated positively with the AMDP schizophrenic syndrome score (P<0.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column Ketamine blood level (p. 11); Results, Plasma ketamine levels (3.1) (p. 14)
key_findings.note: The per-person syndrome scores behind that correlation are not printed. For the two global scores that are printed in Table 1, the rank correlation with plasma level runs the other way and is not significant (editors' calculation: Spearman rho -0.35 for APZ global, -0.21 for EPI global, n=10).

key_findings.finding: Whole-brain glucose metabolism rose in every participant: mean change from baseline 24.5% (SD 14.3; Wilcoxon P<0.01). Editors' calculation: 95% confidence interval about 14.3% to 34.7%, standardised paired difference about 1.7.
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute whole brain and regional cerebral metabolic rates (3.2), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The increase was largest in the cingulate anterior (34%) and frontal cortex (30-34%) and smaller in the insula (19-23%), parietal (18-25%), somatosensory (19-25%), motor (15-18%) and temporal (16-19%) cortex, with the smallest increase in the occipitomedial cortex (16-17%); all increases were significant at P<0.05 to 0.01 except the left cerebellum, and no decreases were found in any region examined.
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute whole brain and regional cerebral metabolic rates (3.2), 1st paragraph (p. 14); Fig. 3 and its caption (p. 16)

key_findings.finding: The frontal increase (mean of frontomedial and frontolateral) was significantly larger than the increases in the left and right temporal and occipitomedial cortex, insula, putamen and cerebellum and in the left thalamus, motor and parietal cortex (all P<0.05); the cingulate anterior increase was likewise larger than those in the temporomedial and occipitomedial cortex, putamen, left caudate nucleus, thalamus and parietal cortex (all P<0.05).
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute whole brain and regional cerebral metabolic rates (3.2), 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Relative CMRglu (region divided by whole brain) rose bilaterally in the frontolateral cortex and in the left anterior cingulate cortex, with trend-level increases in the right frontomedial and parietal cortex (P<0.06), and fell significantly in the left temporomedial and occipitomedial cortex (P<0.05), with the same direction at trend level on the right (P<0.06).
key_findings.locator: Results, Relative metabolic rates and metabolic ratios (3.3), 1st paragraph (p. 14); Fig. 4 (p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Metabolic ratios (Table 2) shifted towards the front: frontomedial/temporomedial rose from 1.31 (SD 0.08) to 1.44 (SD 0.12) on the left and from 1.41 (SD 0.10) to 1.53 (SD 0.17) on the right (both P<0.05); frontomedial/occipitomedial from 1.04 to 1.14 (left) and 1.06 to 1.16 (right) (both P<0.05); frontolateral/temporomedial from 1.30 to 1.47 (left, P<0.01) and 1.31 to 1.46 (right, P<0.05); frontolateral/putamen from 1.00 to 1.09 and 0.98 to 1.09 (both P<0.01). The frontolateral/caudate, frontolateral/thalamus and frontolateral/parietal increases reached significance in the left hemisphere only, and there were more significant changes, and more at P<0.01, on the left than on the right.
key_findings.locator: Results, Relative metabolic rates and metabolic ratios (3.3), 2nd paragraph (p. 14) continuing on p. 15; Table 2 (p. 17)

key_findings.finding: Ketamine produced depersonalisation, derealisation, hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy on the APZ, EPI and AMDP scales; visual phenomena ranged from pseudohallucinations to elementary and complex hallucinations, and most participants became progressively emotionally withdrawn, with flattened affect and concrete proverb interpretation. In Fig. 5, every ketamine-induced change in the plotted subscales is significant at P<0.01 except dread of ego dissolution (AIA, P<0.05).
key_findings.locator: Results, Psychopathology and correlations with metabolism (3.4), 1st paragraph (p. 15); Fig. 5 and its caption (p. 17)

key_findings.finding: Under ketamine the APZ global score was 37.00 (SD 12.63) and the EPI global score 23.40 (SD 5.85), with wide spread between people (APZ global 18 to 60, EPI global 16 to 30 in Table 1).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, columns APZ global and EPI global

key_findings.finding: Correlations with metabolism, uncorrected and with n=10, run in both directions: oceanic boundlessness correlated positively with absolute (P<0.03) and relative (P<0.06) CMRglu in the right frontomedial cortex and with the right midfrontal/temporomedial ratio (P<0.01); the hallucinatory-disintegrative subscale correlated negatively with absolute and relative frontomedial CMRglu in both hemispheres (P<0.05) and with the frontomedial/occipitomedial ratio bilaterally; the schizophrenic syndrome score correlated positively with putamen CMRglu bilaterally (P<0.05) but negatively with the frontomedial/occipitomedial ratios (P<0.05) and with the right frontolateral/putamen ratio (P<0.01); visionary restructuralization correlated positively with occipitomedial CMRglu (left P<0.07, right P<0.05); apathy correlated positively with the left anterior cingulate (P<0.06), left insula (P<0.02) and both parietal cortices (P<0.01) and with the left frontolateral/putamen ratio (P<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results, Psychopathology and correlations with metabolism (3.4), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 15), continuing in the two columns below Table 2 (p. 17); Table 3 (p. 18); Results, final two paragraphs (p. 19)

key_findings.finding: Under baseline conditions metabolism was higher on the left than the right in the parietal (P<0.01) and sensorimotor cortex (P<0.02), an asymmetry abolished under ketamine; under ketamine a left-greater-than-right asymmetry appeared in the frontolateral (P<0.01) and temporomedial cortex (P<0.05) and the putamen (P<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute whole brain and regional cerebral metabolic rates (3.2), 2nd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the frontal cortex was stimulated more (34%) than the occipital cortex (16%) despite an almost equally high NMDA receptor density, and conclude that the metabolic effects cannot be interpreted as strictly due to NMDA receptor blockade, naming GABAergic, serotonergic and dopaminergic contributions; they also note that the low occipital stimulation may reflect that participants had their eyes closed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, Metabolism (4.2), 1st paragraph (p. 19) and the paragraph on occipital cortex (p. 20)

key_findings.finding: The authors describe the correlational results as only preliminary because of the small sample, and limit the model explicitly: the ketamine-induced psychosis is offered as a model of the beginning of acute endogenous psychotic episodes, "not for schizophrenia as a nosological entity".

The study was open, with a drug-free baseline scan rather than a placebo condition, and participants had been told they would receive a stimulant (d-amphetamine) or a hallucinogenic drug (ketamine or psilocybin) on the two drug days.

The psychopathology ratings and the metabolic image do not cover the same window: the ketamine infusion was started 10 minutes before the FDG injection and the scan ran to about 53 minutes after it, while the AMDP and EPI were rated by the psychiatrist on arrival and immediately after the scan and the APZ was completed after the session as a change score for the scan period.
key_findings.locator: Experimental procedures, Phase I (2.5) and Phase II: PET studies (2.6)
key_findings.note: Every correlation in Table 3 therefore sets retrospective ratings of a session against a single integrated metabolic image; the paper does not state this as a limit.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion refers to the ketamine amount used in this study as 1.8 mg/kg and contrasts it with 0.5 mg/kg in other work, but the Methods give only the 20 mg induction step and an infusion rate range of 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min over 60 min, and the paper never reconciles the two. Editors' calculation: 0.03 mg/kg/min, the top of the printed range, over the 60-minute maintenance phase is exactly 1.8 mg/kg, so the Discussion's figure is the maximum of a range and leaves out the induction step.
reporting_issues.consequence: The single amount quoted in the Discussion is not what every participant received and does not include the induction step; the infusion rates and induction amount as printed in the Methods are the only checkable description of the study condition.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 2.1 reports 15 volunteers (8 men, 7 women, mean age 33.3, SD 4.8), but Table 1 and every analysis in the paper cover only the 10 who received ketamine (6 men, 4 women, mean age 33.40, SD 3.57). The sample sentence and the sample actually analysed are three pages apart, and only Table 2 and Table 3 carry n=10 in their headings.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper is easy to read as a study of 15 people; every result in it rests on 10, which matters for any claim about precision.

reporting_issues.issue: The significant positive correlation reported between plasma ketamine level and the AMDP schizophrenic syndrome score cannot be checked from the paper: per-person syndrome scores are not printed, no coefficient is given, and for the two global scores that are printed in Table 1 the rank correlations with plasma level are negative and not significant (editors' calculation: Spearman rho -0.35 for APZ global and -0.21 for EPI global, n=10).
reporting_issues.consequence: A dose-response or concentration-response claim cannot be supported from this paper; the one printed concentration-symptom relation runs in the opposite direction to the one the text reports for a different score.

reporting_issues.issue: The percentage increases in the ratios given in the text (frontomedial/occipitomedial 9-14%, frontomedial/temporomedial 8-12%) cannot be reproduced from the means printed in Table 2 for those rows (editors' calculation from Table 2: about 9.4% and 9.6% for frontomedial/occipitomedial and about 8.5% and 9.9% for frontomedial/temporomedial, so the tops of the stated ranges match the frontolateral rows, about 12-13%, rather than the frontomedial rows named).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text probably reports means of individual percentage changes, which need not equal the change in the means, but the paper does not say so; the table values should be used, and the ranges in the text should not be quoted as if they belonged to the named ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the column FPI neuroticism, a baseline personality score measured before any drug, is printed under the spanning header Ketamine condition, while FPI openness sits under Baseline condition.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader could take the neuroticism score for a drug-condition measure; the text makes clear it is a screening variable.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table 2 defines GA as cingulate anterior, but no row of Table 2 contains that region; the abbreviation is used in Table 3 (FM/GA) on the next page, whose footnote defines it again.
reporting_issues.consequence: Housekeeping only; the frontomedial/anterior cingulate ratio, which carries the ego-identity correlation, is absent from the table of ratio changes, so its baseline and ketamine values are nowhere printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Dispersion is shown three different ways in the three figures of results (Fig. 3 mean plus SD, Fig. 4 mean plus or minus SD, Fig. 5 boxes including 75% of cases), and the caption of Fig. 4 directs the reader to Fig. 2 for the legend, but Fig. 2 is a PET image whose caption carries no abbreviations; the abbreviations are in the caption of Fig. 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Values read from the figures are not comparable with each other, and the regional abbreviations in Fig. 4 have to be taken from a different caption than the one named.

reporting_issues.issue: The column of Table 3 headed Correlation (Spearman) P-level holds P-values carrying the sign of the correlation, not coefficients; no correlation coefficient is printed anywhere in the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction and the significance of each association can be read, but not its size; no claim resting on this paper may state how strongly symptoms and metabolism were related. The same column in the companion paper's Table 2 is mislabelled as r(sp), so the two tables must be read the same way.

disagreements.first_pass: The Discussion refers to the higher doses of ketamine used in this study as 1.8 mg/kg and contrasts them with 0.5 mg/kg in other work, but no total amount appears in the Methods, which give only the 20 mg induction step and the infusion rate range of 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min over 60 min, and the paper never states how 1.8 mg/kg was arrived at or whether it includes the induction step. | The study condition cannot be compared exactly with other laboratories' conditions, and a reader quoting 1.8 mg/kg would be quoting a figure that the methods neither state nor support; the infusion rates and induction amount as printed are the only checkable description.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 226, corrected: how 1.8 mg/kg was arrived at is recoverable, because 0.03 mg/kg/min over the 60-minute maintenance phase is exactly 1.8 mg/kg; the point to keep is that it is the maximum of a range and leaves out the induction step.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted and recomputed (0.03 x 60 = 1.8 mg/kg). The issue was rewritten so that it rests on the figure being the top of a range rather than on it being unrecoverable; the consequence is unchanged in substance.
